current_activity: assaulting Gold Beach and linking with I Corps
notes: Assault corps (Bucknall) at Gold; overran 716th Division and linked with I Corps by end of D-Day (Wikipedia); 7th Armoured followed.
Bulk of 7th Armoured landed 7 June; XXX Corps secured remaining D-Day objectives incl. Bayeux and Port-en-Bessin.

current_activity: attacking Tilly-sur-Seulles; checked by Panzer Lehr
notes: 7th Armoured took over part of 50th Division front 10 June; attacks at Tilly-sur-Seulles checked by Panzer Lehr 10-11 June; XXX Corps had linked with US V Corps by 10 June.

current_activity: advancing via Caumont gap; ambushed at Villers-Bocage
notes: 22nd Armoured Brigade (7th Armoured) reached Villers-Bocage 13 June via the Caumont gap, ambushed (Wittmann); brigade box formed 14 June near Hill 174; offensive suspended.
Re-entered Tilly-sur-Seulles 18 June (changed hands 23 times) and consolidated 19 June; storm 19 June postponed further attacks.

current_activity: launching Operation Martlet against Panzer Lehr and 12th SS
notes: XXX Corps launched Operation Martlet 25 June (49th Div + 8th Armd Bde) vs junction of Panzer Lehr and 12th SS; Fontenay not taken day one.
49th Division took Rauray 16:00 27 June; high ground to the south remained German.

current_activity: Bluecoat: the 43rd Division is to take Point 361 on Mont Pincon and the 50th the Amaye feature; a baffling first day
notes: Event date: 30 July 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 388, 390, 391). Event definition: XXX Corps attacks on the left of the Caumont sector: the 43rd Division is to take Point 361 at the western end of the Mont Pincon ridge and the 50th Division the Amaye-sur-Seulles feature; mines and ground make 30 July an unrewarding and rather baffling day for the corps (pp. 388-390). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 388: "This was to be the first day's objective of XXX Corps' 43rd Division while the 50th Division secured the Amaye sur Seulles feature near Villers-Bocage on its left flank"; pp. 390-391: "It had been an unrewarding and rather baffling day for XXX Corps". Location: Mont Pincon, Calvados (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is Mont Pincon, the ridge whose western end (Point 361) was the first-day objective; the corps did not reach it on 30 July. Location support: Ellis names Point 361 at the western end of the Mont Pincon ridge as the objective of the corps (p. 388).

current_activity: Lt.-Gen. Horrocks takes over the corps from Lt.-Gen. Bucknall; the corps faces south-east from Villers-Bocage
notes: Event date: 4 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 400, 401, 402, 409). Event definition: On 4 August Lt.-Gen. B. G. Horrocks, from England, succeeds Lt.-Gen. G. C. Bucknall in command of XXX Corps, which on 3 August faces south-east from Villers-Bocage to the outskirts of Ondefontaine; the 7th Armoured Division changes commander on the same day. Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, pp. 400-402: "On the 4th of August, Lieut-General B. G. Horrocks (from England) succeeded Lieut- General G. C. Bucknall in command of XXX Corps"; p. 409: "XXX Corps, further west, was left on August the 3rd facing south- east from Villers-Bocage to the outskirts of Ondefontaine". Location: Villers-Bocage (existing place PL0373) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is Villers-Bocage, on the corps front; it is not the corps headquarters. Location support: Ellis names Villers-Bocage as the left of the corps front on 3 August (p. 409); the corps headquarters is not named. Commander: Lt.-Gen. B. G. Horrocks, who succeeded Lt.-Gen. G. C. Bucknall in command of XXX Corps on 4 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 400; named again on pp. 453 and 469).

current_activity: Starts eastwards from the Chambois area; its 11th Armoured Division reaches the Touques near Gace by evening
notes: Event date: 21 August 1944, evening (Ellis, vol. I, p. 453). Event definition: As the American XIX Corps moves north from Verneuil, XXX Corps starts eastwards from the Chambois area on 21 August and its 11th Armoured Division reaches the Touques near Gace that evening; Laigle is occupied on the 22nd, a second division is deployed on the 23rd and the third, the 43rd, which is to force the Seine at Vernon, begins to advance on the 24th (p. 453). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 453: "General Horrocks' XXX Corps started east- wards from the Chambois area; its 11th Armoured Division reached the Touques near Gac"; "On the 23rd XXX Corps was able to deploy a second division". Location: Gacé, Orne (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Ellis names the Touques near Gace as reached on the evening of 21 August (p. 453). Commander: Lt.-Gen. B. G. Horrocks, who succeeded Lt.-Gen. G. C. Bucknall in command of XXX Corps on 4 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 400; named again on pp. 453 and 469).

current_activity: Opens fire across the Seine at Vernon; a battalion and a half of the 43rd Division cross by stormboat during the night
notes: Event date: 25 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 466). Event definition: On 25 August the guns and mortars of XXX Corps open fire across the Seine from Vernon and, fifteen minutes later, the first troops of the 43rd Division cross in stormboats; seven of eight boats are lost, but a battalion and a half cross during the night and sappers bridge the river, a light bridge being completed by the late afternoon of 26 August (p. 466). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 466: "August the 25th, guns and mortars of XXX Corps opened fire on the enemy positions across the Seine from Vernon"; "a battalion and a half crossed during the night". Location: Vernon, Eure (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Ellis names Vernon as the crossing place of the corps (p. 466). Commander: Lt.-Gen. B. G. Horrocks, who succeeded Lt.-Gen. G. C. Bucknall in command of XXX Corps on 4 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 400; named again on pp. 453 and 469).

current_activity: Market Garden: breaks out of the Neerpelt bridgehead for Arnhem; the foremost troops reach Valkenswaard by 19:30
notes: Event date: 17 September 1944, 19:30 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 30, 31, 34). Event definition: On Sunday 17 September XXX Corps starts north from its bridgehead over the Meuse-Escaut canal near Neerpelt along the road through Eindhoven, St. Oedenrode, Veghel, Grave and Nijmegen to Arnhem, with the Guards Armoured Division leading; after a hard fight with anti-tank guns and bazookas the foremost troops reach Valkenswaard at 19:30 and halt there for the night (pp. 30-31 and 34). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 30-31: "The road to be taken by Second Army's XXX Corps started from their small bridgehead over the Meuse"; p. 34: "it was 7.30 p.m. when Valkenswaard was reached by the foremost troops". Location: Valkenswaard, Noord-Brabant (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Ellis names Valkenswaard as reached by the foremost troops that evening (p. 34); the corps headquarters is not named. Commander: Lt.-Gen. B. G. Horrocks, who succeeded Lt.-Gen. G. C. Bucknall in command of XXX Corps on 4 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 400; named again on pp. 453 and 469).

composing_text: US-INF-084D (84th US Infantry Division, temporarily under the corps for the attack); UK-INF-043D (43rd Division, attacking on the left)
current_activity: Clipper: attacks Geilenkirchen and the villages on the Wurm with the US 84th Division under command
notes: Event date: 18 November 1944 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 161, 162). Event definition: On 18 November, two days after the American XIX Corps attacks towards Julich and Linnich, XXX Corps attacks Geilenkirchen and a string of villages astride the Wurm river about three miles further east; the United States 84th Division (temporarily under the corps) attacks on the right with British flail and gun tanks and is through the Siegfried Line pill-boxes by midday, and the 43rd Division then attacks on its left; some 800 prisoners are taken on the first day and Geilenkirchen is captured the next day after a stiff fight (pp. 161-162). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 161-162: "Two days later the British XXX Corps attacked Geilen- kirchen and a string of villages astride the Wurm river about three miles further east"; "The United States 84th Division (temporarily under command of the British XXX Corps), assisted by British flail and gun tanks, attacked on the right and was through the Siegfried Line pill-boxes by midday"; "Next day Geilenkirchen was captured after a stiff fight". Location: Geilenkirchen, North Rhine-Westphalia (existing place PL0558) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the town of Geilenkirchen, the principal objective; the corps headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names Geilenkirchen as the town attacked (p. 161); the corps headquarters is not named. Context: Flagged addition: a 1944 row added in British Batch 2 only so that the existing OP-CLIPPER (Wikipedia, R501) has a British claim next to the US 84th Division row C0544; Ellis does not name the operation.

current_activity: Ardennes: ordered, though not in action, to cover the exits from the Meuse in the Wavre-Tirlemont-Tongres areas
notes: Event date: by 20 December 1944 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 184, 190, 191). Event definition: In the German counter-offensive Field-Marshal Montgomery, ordered on 20 December to take control of the northern battlefield, has already ordered XXX Corps, which is not in action, to take positions covering exits from the Meuse in the Wavre, Tirlemont and Tongres areas with reconnaissance forces forward, and the 29th Armoured Brigade to defend the Meuse bridges at Givet, Dinant and Namur; the corps is to relieve VII Corps for the northern counter-attack (pp. 184 and 190); the order is dated by the day Montgomery took control, so 20 December is the latest possible date (inferred value). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 184: "On the 2oth, when he was ordered to take control of the northern battlefield"; "to take positions covering exits from the Meuse in the Wavre—Tirlemont—Tongres areas with reconnaissance forces forward"; pp. 190-191: "VII Corps would be relieved by the British XXX Corps". Location: Tienen (Tirlemont), Flemish Brabant (new place), the middle of the three areas with a precision of 25 km. Location approximate: the point is Tienen (Tirlemont), the middle of the Wavre-Tirlemont-Tongres line; the corps was to cover this whole area. Location support: Ellis names the areas Wavre, Tirlemont and Tongres (p. 184); the corps headquarters is not named. Commander: Lt.-Gen. B. G. Horrocks, who succeeded Lt.-Gen. G. C. Bucknall in command of XXX Corps on 4 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 400; named again on pp. 453 and 469).

current_activity: Ardennes: attacks south-east from the Marche sector, which it relieved from the US VII Corps; two divisions
notes: Event date: 3 January 1945 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 190, 191). Event definition: On 3 January Montgomery's counter-attack from the north begins; the main attack is by the American First Army's VII Corps south-eastwards towards Houffalize, supported on its right by a simultaneous attack by XXX Corps, which has relieved the American VII Corps in the Marche sector; the British attack is made by two divisions (the 6th Airborne on the right and the 53rd on the left) supported by three army groups of artillery; a thaw bringing mist and mud makes the first day's progress slow and a severe frost and snow then make it slower (pp. 190-191). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 190-191: "On the 3rd of January Montgomery's counter-attack from the north began"; "by the British XXX Corps which had relieved the American VII Corps in the Marche sector"; "The British attack was made by two divisions supported by three army groups of artillery". Location: Marche-en-Famenne, Luxembourg (existing place PL0210), the centre of the Marche sector with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the town of Marche-en-Famenne, the named centre of the sector; the page gives no front line and the corps headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names the Marche sector as the ground the corps took over and attacked from (p. 190).

current_activity: Veritable: transferred to First Canadian Army, disposed behind the northern front to lead the attack
notes: Event date: 7 February 1945 (the German map date; the corps is already in place) (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 254, 255). Event definition: The German OKW situation map of 7 February shows XXX Corps and its formations either unlocated or still south of Roermond; in fact the corps had been transferred to the First Canadian Army and was disposed immediately behind the northern front ready to lead the coming attack; some British divisions, tank brigades and artillery groups began leaving the Ardennes on 18 January but others, from the Blackcock area, could not start before the end of the month; the final moves into the assembly area, whose forward limit was the front between Boxmeer and Nijmegen, were delayed to the last possible moment and made in darkness (pp. 254-255). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 254: "In fact XXX Corps had been transferred to"; p. 255: "the First Canadian Army and was disposed immediately behind the northern front ready to lead the coming attack"; "Some British divisions, tank brigades and artillery groups began leaving the Ardennes on the 18th of January". Location: Nijmegen, Gelderland (existing place PL0554), the town at the centre of the Maas-Rhine assembly area with a precision of 25 km. Location approximate: the point is Nijmegen, the town at the north end of the front between Boxmeer and Nijmegen; the corps headquarters is not named and the concentration area ran from Louvain and Antwerp to Helmond and s-Hertogenbosch. Location support: Ellis gives the assembly area as behind the front between Boxmeer and Nijmegen (p. 255) and names no corps headquarters town.

current_activity: Veritable: 05:00 artillery programme; at 10:30 the barrage lifts and the corps attack towards the Reichswald begins
notes: Event date: 8 February 1945, 05:00 to 10:30 (Ellis, vol. II, p. 257). Event definition: Operation Veritable opens on 8 February: at five in the morning the artillery begins a programme of about 1,050 pieces, the heaviest concentration the British had used in the war; at 10:30 the full barrage makes its first lift and the advance begins; the initial assault and the first phase (the clearing of the Reichswald and the securing of the line Gennep-Asperden-Cleve) are the responsibility of XXX Corps under General Horrocks, led by brigade groups of the 51st, 53rd and 15th Divisions and the Canadian 2nd and 3rd Divisions (the 3rd starting in the evening) (pp. 256-257). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 257: "At five in the morning of February the 8th the artillery opened a programme"; "At 10.30 a.m. the full barrage made its first lift and the advance began"; "The initial assault and completion of the first phase was the responsibility of XXX Corps". Location: Reichswald (forest), North Rhine-Westphalia (existing place PL0698), the first objective of the corps with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the centre of the Reichswald, the first objective; the start line ran from the Maas near Gennep to the Rhine and the corps headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names the clearing of the Reichswald as the first phase of the corps task (p. 256). Commander: General Horrocks, the XXX Corps commander (Ellis, vol. II, p. 256).

current_activity: Rhineland: the corps headquarters reverts to Second Army on the evening of 8 March; its front is near Alpen
notes: Event date: the evening of 8 March 1945 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 276, 277, 278, 279). Event definition: As the front narrows and divisions are stood down, control of all Anglo-Canadian operations passes to General Simonds and, on the evening of 8 March, the Headquarters of XXX Corps reverts to the Second Army; the corps front is then on the Alpen-Menzelen line, with the 53rd Division in the forest south of Alpen by the evening of the 6th, the Guards Armoured Division near Menzelen and the 52nd Division, which clears Alpen, by the 9th (pp. 276-277). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 277-279: "on the evening of March the 8th, the Headquarters of XXX Corps reverted to the Second Army"; p. 276: "By the evening of the 6th, as the Americans reached Rheinberg, the 53rd Division was in the large forest to the south of Alpen". Location: Alpen, North Rhine-Westphalia (new place), on the corps front with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is Alpen, where the divisions of the corps fought in the days before and after; the corps headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names no headquarters town; the corps front is shown by Alpen, where its divisions fought on 6 to 9 March (p. 276). Commander: General Horrocks, the XXX Corps commander (Ellis, vol. II, p. 256).
